notes.meaning: The Lord appeared to Abraham near the large oak trees of Mamre during the hottest part of the day. Abraham was resting at the entrance of his tent to catch any cool breeze that blew by. This quiet visit showed God drawing near in a personal and friendly way to encourage His servant.

Abraham looked up and saw three travellers standing nearby, so he quickly ran out to welcome them with a deep bow. He greeted them with great respect according to ancient customs of hospitality, before he even realized who they truly were. Two of the visitors were angels, and one was the Lord Himself appearing in human form.

differ.view: Anglicans historically read this passage on Trinity Sunday because the three visitors reflect the three persons of God, though commentators caution this does not prove the Trinity.

notes.meaning: Abraham addressed the leader among the visitors as my lord and begged them not to pass him by without stopping. He considered it a great privilege to care for these weary travellers. He asked them to accept his hospitality as a sign of favour toward him.

Abraham offered to bring water so the travellers could wash the dust from their feet and rest under the shade of the tree. In that hot and dry country, people wore sandals, so washing a guest's feet was the very first act of kindness. Resting in the cool shade gave them time to recover from the midday heat.

Abraham promised to bring out a small bite of bread so his guests could regain their energy before moving on. Though he spoke humbly of giving just a little bread, he was planning a grand feast for them. The visitors graciously accepted his kind offer to rest and eat.

Abraham hurried into the tent to tell Sarah to make fresh bread right away. He asked her to use three large measures of fine flour, knead the dough, and bake flat cakes over the hot coals. Even though Abraham was a wealthy master, he and his wife gladly did the hard work of serving their guests themselves.

Abraham then ran out to his herd and picked out a young, tender calf to prepare for meat. Serving meat was a special honour saved only for the most important visitors. He gave the calf to a servant, who quickly prepared and cooked the meal.

Abraham brought out the cooked meat, along with milk and curdled milk, and placed the whole meal before his guests. He stood quietly beside them under the tree like a servant to make sure they had everything they needed. Although the guests were heavenly beings, they really ate the food that was set before them.

The visitors asked Abraham where his wife Sarah was, and he answered that she was inside the tent. In those days, women stayed in the private part of the tent when male strangers visited. By asking for Sarah by name, the visitors showed they already knew all about Abraham and his family.

The Lord announced that He would return in about a year, and Sarah would give birth to a son. Sarah was listening just inside the tent entrance right behind the speaker. This promise renewed God's earlier covenant word and made sure Sarah herself heard the good news.

Abraham and Sarah were both very old and well past the normal time of life for having children. Sarah had already gone through the natural change of life when pregnancy is no longer possible. From a purely human point of view, having a baby was completely out of the question.

Sarah laughed quietly to herself, wondering how she and her elderly husband could possibly have a child now. She did not laugh with joyful faith, but with doubt because nature seemed to make the promise impossible. Even in her doubt, she respectfully called Abraham her master or lord.

The Lord asked Abraham why Sarah had laughed and questioned whether she could really have a child at her age. God spoke directly to Abraham as the leader of the household to address Sarah's secret doubt. Even though Sarah had laughed silently inside her own heart, God knew her thoughts perfectly.

The Lord asked if anything is too hard or wonderful for Him to do. He repeated His promise that He would return at the set time next year and Sarah would hold a baby boy. This showed that God's almighty power is never limited by the normal laws of nature.

Sarah became frightened because her secret thoughts were known, so she lied and said she had not laughed. The Lord gently but firmly corrected her by saying she truly did laugh. God showed her that nothing can be hidden from Him, yet He did not take away His promise because of her weakness.

The heavenly visitors stood up and looked out toward the city of Sodom, and Abraham walked along with them to send them on their journey. Walking partway with departing guests was an ancient sign of respect and warm friendship. This walk brought Abraham into position to hear what God planned to do next.

The Lord paused and asked whether He should keep His upcoming plans secret from Abraham. God spoke in this human way to show how close His friendship was with Abraham. He decided to share His thoughts with Abraham because of the special relationship between them.

God explained that Abraham would certainly grow into a great and powerful nation, and all the nations on earth would be blessed through him. Because Abraham was chosen to carry this worldwide blessing, God treated him as a trusted partner. Knowing God's judgments would help Abraham's descendants understand God's holy ways.

The Lord declared that He had chosen Abraham so that he would teach his children and his entire household to live right and obey God. God values parents who guide their families to worship Him and treat others fairly. Walking in God's ways allows His promises to be passed down from one generation to the next.

differ.view: Baptists emphasize that this passage places the primary duty of spiritual and moral training on parents in the home, rather than on the church or government.

notes.meaning: The Lord told Abraham that the cry against Sodom and Gomorrah was loud and their sin was extremely terrible. The word cry means that the wickedness and cruelty in those cities called out to heaven for justice. God does not overlook evil, and when human wrongdoing reaches its limit, He steps in to judge it.

The Lord said He would go down to see for Himself if the people were as completely wicked as the reports showed. God already knows all things, but He spoke like a human judge to show that His punishment would be fair, careful, and fully deserved. This taught Abraham that God never judges rashly or without proof.

Two of the visitors turned and walked on toward Sodom, but Abraham stayed standing before the Lord. The two who walked away were angels sent to carry out God's work, while the one who stayed was the Lord Himself. Abraham took this quiet moment to speak to God on behalf of the endangered people.

Abraham stepped forward and asked the Lord if He would really destroy good people along with the wicked. He began the very first recorded prayer of intercession, which means praying to God on behalf of other people. Abraham cared deeply about human life and wanted to see God's mercy at work.

Abraham asked if the Lord would spare the whole city if fifty righteous people lived there. He pleaded that the entire place might be saved for the sake of those few faithful residents. He hoped that even in a corrupt place, some people who feared God could be found.

Abraham declared that destroying the righteous together with the wicked would be completely against God's nature. He called God the Judge of all the earth and stated with confidence that God would always do what is right. Abraham based his bold prayer on God's own perfect justice and goodness.

The Lord answered that if He found fifty righteous people in the city of Sodom, He would spare the entire place for their sake. God showed how ready He is to show mercy to many for the sake of a few godly people. This answer gave Abraham hope and encouraged him to keep praying.

Abraham answered with deep humility, confessing that he was only dust and ashes before the Lord. He realized how small and frail he was compared to the great and glorious Creator. True prayer combines bold requests with deep respect and humble hearts.

Abraham asked if God would destroy the whole city if only forty-five righteous people were found instead of fifty. He wondered if missing just five people would cause God to wipe out the city. The Lord kindly replied that He would not destroy it if forty-five righteous people were there.

Abraham spoke up again and asked what would happen if forty righteous people were found. The Lord answered that He would spare the city for the sake of forty. Each time Abraham asked for more mercy, God patiently granted his request.

Abraham asked the Lord not to be angry as he continued to plead, asking what would happen if thirty were found. God answered that He would not destroy the city if thirty righteous people lived there. Abraham's persistent requests showed how deeply he desired to see lives saved.

Abraham acknowledged once more his boldness in speaking to the Lord, and he asked about the number twenty. The Lord promised that He would not destroy the city on account of twenty righteous people. God's patience remained steady even as the number grew smaller and smaller.

Finally, Abraham asked the Lord not to be angry for one last request, asking if the city would be spared for ten righteous people. The Lord promised that even for ten, He would not destroy it. Abraham stopped at ten, likely hoping that his nephew Lot and Lot's household would be enough to meet that number.

When the Lord finished talking with Abraham, He departed, and Abraham went back home to his tent. God had stayed and listened until Abraham had said everything in his heart. Although Sodom was later destroyed because not even ten righteous people were there, God heard Abraham's prayer and rescued Lot.
